extracted.intended_audience: academics, researchers, and early-career scholars who perform peer review for journals/conferences
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for scholars on how to perform constructive peer review of academic articles (when to accept/decline invitations, how to structure reading and comments, tone to use, and what to prioritise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sure you are the right person for the article
rubrics_metrics.description: Only accept review requests when you have sufficient knowledge of the paper's themes and methods; politely decline if you don't feel confident in the methodology or field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't need to be an expert in every aspect of a paper to review it, but you should have some knowledge of its themes and methods. If you have studied the method at a Masters level or have read several works cited in the bibliography, you're probably competent enough. Use your own judgement about your abilities; if lacking, decline rather than provide an unhelpful review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be in the right frame of mind to review
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept reviews when you are overloaded, stressed, or otherwise distracted — these states will negatively affect review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't say yes if you are snowed under with marking, examining, grant bids, or similar tasks. Reviewing should be pleasurable and a chance to read cutting-edge work. Do the review in stages: first read and take small notes; second re-read and formulate useful comments; third type up responses and include links. Taking these staged steps helps produce a higher-quality, less rushed review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review as you would want to be reviewed (tone & attitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give authors the benefit of the doubt and avoid heavy-handed, aggressive, or admonishing language; treat authors as peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of writing condemnatory statements (e.g., 'The authors clearly aren't aware...'), use constructive wording (e.g., 'Citing X in paragraph 2, page 4 would probably support this aspect of your argument'). If you are genuinely frustrated with a manuscript, vent to colleagues rather than putting malice in the review — harsh tone only harms authors and makes you look bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on high-level (substantive) comments over low-level copyediting
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritise 'high comments' (theme, engagement with literature, methodological goodness-of-fit) rather than minor issues like grammar or formatting, which are usually handled by copy editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High comments should assess appropriateness of theory, literature engagement, and methodological fit. Reserve notes about grammar/spelling/format for secondary, limited comments; the main value reviewers add is substantive critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific and provide actionable suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: When critiquing an aspect (e.g., analysis, literature engagement), explain why it's problematic, state what is missing, and suggest concrete alternatives or fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague remarks such as 'analysis problematic' or 'doesn't engage with the literature.' Specify what is missing, name particular works or theorists, and, when suggesting inclusion of a work, provide a full citation (author+year+title or link) rather than an ambiguous short form (e.g., not just 'Brown 2015'). Where possible, include links to recommended sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common 'Reviewer #2' anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not behave in the ways typified by the stereotype 'Reviewer #2' — grumpy, aggressive, vague, unhelpful, dogmatic about a pet discipline or methodology, inflexible, unwilling to give benefit of the doubt, or unwilling to treat authors as peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post lists the following qualities to avoid: 'Grumpy; Aggressive; Vague; Unhelpful; Overbearingly committed to a pet discipline; Overly focused on a particular methodology; Inflexible; Unwilling to give the benefit of the doubt; Unwilling to view the authors of a submitted paper as peers.' Examples of bad reviews can be found on aggregator sites (e.g., 'Shit My Reviewers Say') and should be used as cautionary exemplars of what not to do.
